facts.text: Taiwan's household power is 110 volts at 60 hertz.
Taiwan uses Type A plugs (two flat pins) and Type B plugs (the North American three-pin plug); many buildings also have 220-volt sockets for air conditioners.
Japan's household power is 100 volts everywhere; eastern Japan uses 50 hertz and western Japan, including Nagoya, Kyoto and Osaka, uses 60 hertz.
Japan uses Type A plugs, which have two flat pins, and Japanese sockets usually have no hole for a grounding pin.
Eastern Japan built its power grid on the German 50-hertz system, while western Japan followed the American 60-hertz system.
Homes in the United States get about 120 volts at 60 hertz; many other countries use 220 to 240 volts at 50 hertz.
American plugs with two flat pins fit Japanese sockets; a U.S. three-prong plug with a grounding pin is called Type B.
South Korea's standard power is 220 volts at 60 hertz, and its sockets are Types C and F, which take plugs with two round pins.
Germany's standard power is 230 volts at 50 hertz, and its sockets are Type F (Schuko) and Type C.
Switzerland's standard power is 230 volts at 50 hertz; it uses Type C (two-pin) and Type J (three-pin) sockets.
The UK supply is 230 volts at 50 hertz; UK plugs have three pins and must be fitted with a fuse of 13 amps or less.
Australia's mains power is 230 volts at 50 hertz, and it uses Type I plugs with three flat pins.
Electrical standards were first set by each country on its own, at a time when there was no international standard.
Early household appliances had to be wired directly into a building's electric system; there was no easy way to plug them in.
American inventor Harvey Hubbell designed a separable attachment plug; its patent is dated June 17, 1913. His first plug went into a light socket.
In the 1880s, the voltage delivered to American homes was set at 110 volts.
European power companies found that supplying power at 220 volts instead of 110 volts was cheaper.
In 1899 the Berlin power company BEW raised its voltage from 110 to 220 volts, and this spread across Europe over the following decades.
About 15 different types of household plugs are in use around the world; their letter names come from the U.S. Department of Commerce.
A plug adaptor only lets a plug fit a different socket; it does not change the voltage.
Many laptops and phone chargers are dual-voltage, usually marked 100–240 V, so they need only a plug adaptor abroad.
Engineers developed the grounding pin in the 1920s to make plugs safer; it became the U.S. home standard only in 1971.

notes: 旅遊表格（8 個國家或地區的電壓、頻率、插頭型式）依 s1–s12 各國政府觀光／商務頁面與大學給國際學生的說明整理；英國的插頭型式字母（G）在可取得的來源中沒有逐字出現，表格改寫成「三個插腳、插頭內有保險絲」。美國的 Type A 由 s12（美國兩腳插頭可直接插日本插座）與 s2（日本是 Type A）推得。各地電壓為標稱值（英國、澳洲標稱 230 V，實際常接近 240 V）。
